claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: To induce a learned decrease in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the same direction.
claims.source: To induce a learned increase in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the opposite direction (Figure 2A); to induce a learned decrease in VOR gain, visual image motion is paired with a vestibular stimulus in the same direction (Figure 2B; Collewijn and Grootendorst, 1979; Vercher and Gauthier, 1990–1991; Pastor et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Most climbing fibers in the flocculus increase their firing in response to contraversive retinal slip.
claims.source: Most climbing fibers in the flocculus increase their firing in response to contraversive retinal slip (image motion away from the side on which the cell is recorded) (Simpson and Alley, 1974; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Stone and Lisberger, 1990; Figure 2C–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claims.claim: During VOR-increase training, the contraversive retinal slip that activates climbing fibers occurs during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli.
claims.source: During VOR-increase training, the contraversive retinal slip that activates climbing fibers occurs during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2A,C,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,E), whereas during VOR-decrease training, the contraversive retinal slip and associated increase in climbing fiber activity occur during contraversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: During VOR-decrease training, the contraversive retinal slip and associated increase in climbing fiber activity occur during contraversive vestibular stimuli.
claims.source: During VOR-increase training, the contraversive retinal slip that activates climbing fibers occurs during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2A,C,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,E), whereas during VOR-decrease training, the contraversive retinal slip and associated increase in climbing fiber activity occur during contraversive vestibular stimuli (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The amplitude of the climbing fiber response to retinal slip is the same during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.
claims.source: The same climbing fibers encode retinal slip during both training paradigms, and the amplitude of the response is the same (Figure 2E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2E,F.

claims.claim: What distinguishes VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training is whether the increased climbing fiber activity occurs during vestibular stimuli in one direction vs the other.
claims.source: What distinguishes the two paradigms, and carries information about the required direction of learning, is whether the increased climbing fiber activity occurs during vestibular stimuli in one direction vs the other.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing the two training paradigms.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output through long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses.
claims.source: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output, either through long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (Ito et al., 1982) or through potentiation of inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cell (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output through potentiation of inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cell.
claims.source: Climbing fiber-induced plasticity can reduce Purkinje cell simple spike output, either through long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (Ito et al., 1982) or through potentiation of inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cell (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A reduction in Purkinje cell firing during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli would cause VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei to receive inhibition from Purkinje cells that is more out-of-phase with the excitatory input they receive from vestibular afferents, leading to larger responses in the vestibular nuclei and an increase in VOR gain.
claims.source: A reduction in Purkinje cell firing during ipsiversive vestibular stimuli would cause VOR interneurons in the vestibular nuclei to receive inhibition from Purkinje cells that is more out-of-phase with the excitatory input they receive from vestibular afferents (Figure 1), leading to larger responses in the vestibular nuclei and hence an increase in VOR gain (Ito, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: A climbing fiber-triggered reduction in Purkinje cell firing during contraversive vestibular stimuli would cause the inhibition from Purkinje cells to be more in-phase with the excitatory vestibular afferents, resulting in smaller responses of vestibular nuclei neurons and a decrease in VOR gain.
claims.source: In contrast, a climbing fiber-triggered reduction in Purkinje cell firing during contraversive vestibular stimuli would cause the inhibition from Purkinje cells to be more in-phase with the excitatory vestibular afferents, resulting in smaller responses of vestibular nuclei neurons and a decrease in VOR gain.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on inference from the circuit architecture.

claims.claim: Changes in Purkinje cell responses consistent with climbing fiber-triggered plasticity have been reported by several laboratories after VOR learning.
claims.source: Such changes in Purkinje cell responses have been reported by several laboratories after VOR learning (Dufossé et al., 1978; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger et al., 1994; Miles et al., 1980; Nagao, 1989; Watanabe, 1984, 1985).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: If there was a spike in the climbing fiber input on the first trial of a pair during VOR-increase training, there was a reduction of about 8 spikes/s in the firing rate of the Purkinje cell on the subsequent trial.
claims.source: If there was a spike in the climbing fiber input on the first trial of a pair, there was a reduction of about 8 spikes/s in the firing rate of the Purkinje cell on the subsequent trial (Figure 3B,C; CF–No CF, red).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: On trials with no climbing fiber spike during VOR-increase training, there was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing rate on the subsequent trial.
claims.source: On trials with no climbing fiber spike, there was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing rate on the subsequent trial (Figure 3B,C; No CF–No CF, black).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: The sensory error (retinal slip speed) was indistinguishable on trials with a climbing fiber spike vs without a climbing fiber spike.
claims.source: The sensory error (retinal slip speed) was indistinguishable on trials with a climbing fiber spike vs without a climbing fiber spike, and therefore cannot account for the difference observed on the trial after the climbing fiber spike (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The tight, trial-by-trial correlation between the occurrence of a climbing fiber spike on one trial and the change in Purkinje cell simple spike output on the next trial suggests that the activation of the climbing fibers is what is triggering the changes in Purkinje cell output during VOR-increase training.
claims.source: The tight, trial-by-trial correlation between the occurrence of a climbing fiber spike on one trial, and the change in Purkinje cell simple spike output on the next trial suggests that the activation of the climbing fibers is what is triggering the changes in Purkinje cell output during VOR-increase training.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing on the trial after a climbing fiber spike during VOR-decrease training.
claims.source: Unlike VOR-increase training and all previous trial-by-trial analyses of smooth pursuit learning (Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Yang and Lisberger, 2010, 2013), there was no reduction in Purkinje cell firing on the trial after a climbing fiber spike during VOR-decrease training (Figure 3D,E; CF-No CF, blue).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claims.claim: The Purkinje cells underwent gradual, adaptive changes in their responses over the course of VOR-decrease training sessions.
claims.source: The Purkinje cells did undergo gradual, adaptive changes in their responses over the course of the full VOR-decrease training session, which could be detected during the same ∼90-s VOR-decrease training sessions used for the trial-by-trial analysis (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Across trials of VOR-decrease training, there was a progressively lower Purkinje cell firing rate during contraversive vestibular stimuli.
claims.source: Across trials of VOR-decrease training, there was a progressively lower Purkinje cell firing rate during contraversive vestibular stimuli, similar to what has been reported previously using much longer training periods (Dufossé et al., 1978; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Lisberger et al., 1994; Miles, Braitman, et al., 1980; Nagao, 1989; Watanabe, 1984, 1985).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Lesions of the floccular complex disrupt both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning.
claims.source: This observation, along with the observation that lesions of the floccular complex disrupt both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning (Ito et al., 1982; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Lisberger et al., 1984; Nagao, 1983; Rambold and Churchland, 2002), indicates that the Purkinje cells in our sample participate in VOR-decrease learning as well as VOR-increase learning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The Purkinje cells in the sample participate in VOR-decrease learning as well as VOR-increase learning.
claims.source: This observation, along with the observation that lesions of the floccular complex disrupt both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning (Ito et al., 1982; Koekkoek et al., 1997; Lisberger et al., 1984; Nagao, 1983; Rambold and Churchland, 2002), indicates that the Purkinje cells in our sample participate in VOR-decrease learning as well as VOR-increase learning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and previous lesion studies.

claims.claim: Although the performance errors elicited equally robust responses in the climbing fibers during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training, those responses seem to have a different impact in terms of their ability to induce plasticity.
claims.source: Thus, although the performance errors elicited equally robust responses in the climbing fibers during the two learning paradigms, those responses seem to have a different impact in terms of their ability to induce plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing the two training paradigms.

claims.claim: There is robust activation of mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellar flocculus during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli.
claims.source: This seems unlikely because there is robust activation of mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellar flocculus during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Noda, 1986), and a substantial fraction of Purkinje cells increase their firing in response to contraversive vestibular stimuli (Dufossé et al., 1978; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Miles et al., 1980; Watanabe, 1984; Nagao, 1989; Pastor et al, 1997; Lisberger et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1997; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Blazquez et al., 2003; Ke et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: A substantial fraction of Purkinje cells increase their firing in response to contraversive vestibular stimuli.
claims.source: This seems unlikely because there is robust activation of mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellar flocculus during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli (Noda, 1986), and a substantial fraction of Purkinje cells increase their firing in response to contraversive vestibular stimuli (Dufossé et al., 1978; Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Miles et al., 1980; Watanabe, 1984; Nagao, 1989; Pastor et al, 1997; Lisberger et al., 1994; Raymond and Lisberger, 1997; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Blazquez et al., 2003; Ke et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There should be cerebellar synapses coactive with the climbing fibers during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training paradigms.
claims.source: Thus, there should be cerebellar synapses coactive with the climbing fibers during both training paradigms, and therefore some other aspect of the state of the cerebellar circuit is more likely to be regulating the ability of the error signals carried by climbing fibers to induce plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous evidence about mossy fiber and Purkinje cell activity.

claims.claim: When the number of spikelets and complex spike duration are manipulated in vitro or in decerebrate animals, the probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity can be altered, with shorter complex spike durations associated with a lower probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity.
claims.source: When the number of spikelets, and hence the complex spike duration, is manipulated in vitro or in decerebrate animals (Carey and Regehr, 2009; Mathy et al., 2009; Rasmussen et al., 2013), the probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity can be altered, with shorter complex spike durations associated with a lower probability of climbing fiber-induced plasticity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Complex spike waveforms during VOR-decrease training had more spikelets and were of longer duration than those during VOR-increase training.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that complex spike waveforms during VOR-decrease training had more spikelets and were of longer duration than those during VOR-increase training (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The reduced efficacy of climbing fibers to induce plasticity during VOR-decrease learning cannot be explained by a shorter complex spike duration.
claims.source: Thus, the reduced efficacy of climbing fibers to induce plasticity during VOR-decrease learning cannot be explained by a shorter complex spike duration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on complex spike duration.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the duration of the post-complex spike pause during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.
claims.source: However, there was no significant difference in the duration of the post-complex spike pause during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: For both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training, simple spike firing rate decreased relative to baseline during the training stimulus, but this reduction was smaller during VOR-decrease training than VOR-increase training.
claims.source: For both, firing rate decreased relative to baseline during the training stimulus (Figure 2G,H), but this reduction was smaller during VOR-decrease training than VOR-increase training (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 2G,H and 5C.

claims.claim: There is no floor effect limiting plasticity of the simple spike responses during VOR-decrease training.
claims.source: This suggests that there is no floor effect limiting plasticity of the simple spike responses during VOR-decrease training.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simple spike firing rate data.

claims.claim: The difference in simple spike rates during VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training suggests different patterns of excitatory and inhibitory input to Purkinje cells, which might regulate climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the difference in simple spike rates during the two training paradigms suggests different patterns of excitatory and inhibitory input to Purkinje cells, which might regulate climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the simple spike firing rate data.

claims.claim: Virus carrying ChR2 was injected into the inferior olive to optogenetically stimulate climbing fibers.
claims.source: To optogenetically stimulate climbing fibers, virus carrying ChR2 was injected into the inferior olive, and several weeks later, the climbing fiber terminals in the cerebellar flocculus were illuminated with blue light (Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claims.claim: ChR2 expression in the climbing fibers was verified anatomically, and optrode recordings from Purkinje cells demonstrated that complex spikes could be elicited by brief pulses of light to the flocculus.
claims.source: ChR2 expression in the climbing fibers was verified anatomically, and optrode recordings from Purkinje cells demonstrated that complex spikes could be elicited by brief pulses of light to the flocculus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: When climbing fibers were stimulated during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus, the VOR gain was higher than the vestibular-only control at the end of training.
claims.source: If the climbing fibers were stimulated during the ipsiversive phase of the same vestibular stimulus, the VOR gain was higher than the vestibular-only control at the end of training (Figure 6B, red and Figure 7A, pink).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7A.

claims.claim: The effect of climbing fiber stimulation during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus was long-lasting; when retested 2 hr after training, the VOR gain was still higher compared to vestibular-only training.
claims.source: This effect of climbing fiber stimulation was long-lasting; when retested 2 hr after training, the VOR gain was still higher compared to vestibular-only training (Figure 6B, red and Figure 7B, pink).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7B.

claims.claim: For both optogenetic VOR-increase and vestibular-only training paradigms, there was an increase in VOR gain between the end of training and the 2 hr retest, presumably reflecting decay of the non-associative habituation.
claims.source: For both training paradigms, there was an increase in VOR gain between the end of training and the 2 hr retest, presumably reflecting decay of the non-associative habituation (Figure 6B, black and Figure 7, dark grey).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text with a speculative explanation and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7.

claims.claim: Pairing climbing fiber stimulation with the contraversive phase of the vestibular stimulus had no detectable effect on VOR gain, immediately or 2 hr post-training.
claims.source: This pairing had no detectable effect, immediately or 2 hr post-training. There was no significant reduction of the gain of the VOR below the habituation level observed in response to training with the vestibular stimulus alone (Figure 6B, blue and Figure 7, light blue).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6B and 7.

claims.claim: When the vestibular stimulus was paired with an appropriate visual stimulus, there was a bigger decrease in VOR gain than induced by the vestibular stimulus alone, demonstrating that an associative decrease in VOR gain was possible.
claims.source: In contrast, when the vestibular stimulus was paired with an appropriate visual stimulus (see 'Materials and methods'), there was a bigger decrease in VOR gain than induced by the vestibular stimulus alone, demonstrating that an associative decrease in VOR gain was possible (Figure 7A, white).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Stronger climbing fiber stimulation paradigms (three stimuli per cycle, unilateral or bilateral) induced bigger increases in VOR gain when delivered during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus.
claims.source: These stronger climbing fiber stimulation paradigms induced bigger increases in VOR gain when delivered during the ipsiversive phase of the vestibular stimulus (Figure 7, dark pink and red).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: When timed to induce VOR-decrease learning, increasing the number of climbing fiber stimuli had no effect.
claims.source: However, when timed to induce VOR-decrease learning, increasing the number of climbing fiber stimuli had no effect (Figure 7, blue and dark blue).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: None of the optogenetic training paradigms induced a decrease in VOR gain below the vestibular-only control, either immediately or 2 hr after the end of training.
claims.source: Thus, none of our training paradigms induced a decrease in VOR gain below the vestibular-only control, either immediately or 2 hr after the end of training.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claims.claim: The same climbing fiber stimulation protocols were effective at inducing robust and graded learning when timed relative to the vestibular stimulus to mimic VOR-increase training.
claims.source: However, the same climbing fiber stimulation protocols were effective at inducing robust and graded learning when timed relative to the vestibular stimulus to mimic VOR-increase training.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claims.claim: The lack of VOR-decrease learning in response to optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation was consistent with the trial-by-trial analysis, which found no evidence for a contribution of the natural, visually-elicited error signals in the climbing fibers to the induction of VOR-decrease learning.
claims.source: Moreover, the lack of VOR-decrease learning in response to optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation was consistent with the trial-by-trial analysis, which found no evidence for a contribution of the natural, visually-elicited error signals in the climbing fibers to the induction of VOR-decrease learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the optogenetic stimulation results with the trial-by-trial analysis results.

claims.claim: The stimulation results, together with the trial-by-trial recordings, suggest that VOR-decrease learning is not induced by the climbing fibers, even though they carry error signals that could potentially guide learning.
claims.source: Thus, the stimulation results, together with the trial-by-trial recordings, suggest that VOR-decrease learning is not induced by the climbing fibers, even though they carry error signals that could potentially guide learning, and the very same climbing fibers contribute to the induction of VOR-increase learning.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claims.claim: Both recording and stimulation results indicate that during VOR learning, the efficacy of the climbing fibers for inducing plasticity is gated downstream of their encoding of errors.
claims.source: Both our recording and stimulation results indicate that during VOR learning, the efficacy of the climbing fibers for inducing plasticity is gated downstream of their encoding of errors.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claims.claim: The coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity is regulated, and can vary across different learning contexts.
claims.source: In contrast, a comparison of the positive and negative results from the two VOR learning paradigms indicates that the coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity is regulated, and can vary across different learning contexts.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results comparing VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.

claims.claim: The results provide some of the strongest evidence to date that error signals carried by the climbing fibers drive VOR-increase learning.
claims.source: Our results provide some of the strongest evidence to date that error signals carried by the climbing fibers drive VOR-increase learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results for VOR-increase training.

claims.claim: The equally robust error signals carried by the climbing fibers during VOR-decrease training seem to make little or no contribution to the induction of learning.
claims.source: However, the equally robust error signals carried by the climbing fibers during VOR-decrease training seem to make little or no contribution to the induction of learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results for VOR-decrease training.

claims.claim: During VOR-decrease training, the animals are learning.
claims.source: During VOR-decrease training, the animals are learning (Raymond and Lisberger, 1996), and there are changes in the responses of the Purkinje cells that can be detected within the 90-s training period (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The changes in Purkinje cell responses during VOR-decrease training do not seem to be driven by the climbing fibers.
claims.source: However, those changes do not seem to be driven by the climbing fibers, because there was no trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber activity and changes in Purkinje cell simple spike responses of the kind observed during VOR-increase or smooth pursuit learning (Figure 3, Medina and Lisberger, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trial-by-trial analysis results.

claims.claim: In vivo, climbing fiber activity is sometimes a potent trigger for plasticity, but at other times has no effect.
claims.source: Thus, in vivo, climbing fiber activity is sometimes a potent trigger for plasticity, but at other times has no effect.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results comparing VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training.

claims.claim: Gating of the climbing fibers' efficacy for inducing plasticity represents a novel component of the cerebellar learning algorithm.
claims.source: This gating of the climbing fibers' efficacy for inducing plasticity represents a novel component of the cerebellar learning algorithm.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion and interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.claim: The convergent evidence from recording and stimulation experiments, as well as previous perturbation studies, strengthens the interpretation of the results.
claims.source: The convergent evidence from recording and stimulation experiments, as well as previous, perturbation studies, strengthens the interpretation of the results.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach and interpretation of the study.

claims.claim: The current recording and stimulation results are consistent with a previous perturbation study reporting that mice with impaired pf-Pk LTD are selectively impaired on VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning.
claims.source: Moreover, the current recording and stimulation results are consistent with a previous perturbation study reporting that mice with impaired long-term depression of the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (pf-Pk LTD) are selectively impaired on VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning (Boyden et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The present results extend previous work by demonstrating a selective contribution, not only of pf-Pk LTD, but of all climbing fiber-dependent plasticity mechanisms to VOR-increase learning but not VOR-decrease learning.
claims.source: Thus, the present results extend our previous work by demonstrating a selective contribution, not only of pf-Pk LTD, but of all climbing fiber-dependent plasticity mechanisms to VOR-increase learning but not VOR-decrease learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and their interpretation.

claims.claim: The results for VOR-increase learning provide a positive control indicating that the experimental approaches were able to detect climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
claims.source: The results for VOR-increase learning provide a positive control indicating that our experimental approaches were able to detect climbing fiber-triggered plasticity, which is critical for interpreting the negative results from VOR-decrease learning.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and interpretation.

claims.claim: Direct comparison of the VOR-increase and VOR-decrease paradigms provides a demonstration that the very same animals and even the very same cells could toggle between either a tight coupling or no apparent coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity, depending on the behavioral context.
claims.source: In contrast, direct comparison of the VOR-increase and VOR-decrease paradigms provides a demonstration that the very same animals and even the very same cells could toggle between either a tight coupling or no apparent coupling between climbing fiber activity and the induction of plasticity, depending on the behavioral context of the specific oculomotor training paradigm.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Direct comparison of the positive and negative results from VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning in the same animals and the same cells, using the same techniques, suggests that climbing fiber efficacy is actively regulated.
claims.source: Thus, direct comparison of the positive and negative results from VOR-increase and VOR-decrease learning in the same animals and the same cells, using the same techniques, suggests that climbing fiber efficacy is actively regulated.
claims.evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: In vitro, ethanol and neuromodulators such as norepinephrine can affect the duration of a complex spike and the induction of climbing fiber-dependent plasticity.
claims.source: In vitro, ethanol and neuromodulators such as norepinephrine can affect the duration of a complex spike and the induction of climbing fiber-dependent plasticity (Carey and Regehr 2009; He et al., 2013; Belmeguenai et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There was no reduction in complex spike duration during VOR-decrease training that would account for the reduced efficacy of climbing fiber spikes suggested by the trial-by-trial analysis.
claims.source: However, there was no reduction in complex spike duration during VOR-decrease training that would account for the reduced efficacy of climbing fiber spikes suggested by the trial-by-trial analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on complex spike duration.

claims.claim: Coactive inhibitory inputs can impair the induction of LTD at the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses.
claims.source: Another factor that may gate the efficacy of climbing fibers to induce synaptic plasticity is the level of inhibition: coactive inhibitory inputs can impair the induction of LTD at the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (Ekerot and Kano, 1985), but also may serve as a substrate for climbing fiber-induced plasticity (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Inhibitory inputs may serve as a substrate for climbing fiber-induced plasticity.
claims.source: Another factor that may gate the efficacy of climbing fibers to induce synaptic plasticity is the level of inhibition: coactive inhibitory inputs can impair the induction of LTD at the parallel fiber-to-Purkinje cell synapses (Ekerot and Kano, 1985), but also may serve as a substrate for climbing fiber-induced plasticity (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003; Kano et al., 1992; Tanaka et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: During both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training paradigms, simple spike firing rate decreased relative to the spontaneous, pre-stimulus baseline around the time of climbing fiber activation.
claims.source: During both training paradigms, simple spike firing rate decreased relative to the spontaneous, pre-stimulus baseline around the time of climbing fiber activation (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The decrease in simple spike rate was smaller during VOR-decrease than VOR-increase training, indicating a higher ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cells at the time of climbing fiber activity during VOR-decrease vs VOR-increase training.
claims.source: This decrease in simple spike rate was smaller during VOR-decrease than VOR-increase training, indicating a higher ratio of excitatory to inhibitory inputs to the Purkinje cells at the time of climbing fiber activity during VOR-decrease vs VOR-increase training.

results.result: During VOR-increase training, climbing fiber activity on one trial predicted changes in Purkinje cell output on the next trial. A climbing fiber spike on trial n led to an ~8 spikes/s reduction in Purkinje cell firing on trial n+1, while trials without climbing fiber spikes showed no such change. This trial-by-trial correlation was not explained by differences in sensory error (retinal slip).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C57-C60 provide converging evidence from trial-by-trial analysis showing a tight correlation between climbing fiber spikes and subsequent Purkinje cell plasticity during VOR-increase training. The data in Figure 3B,C demonstrate the effect with appropriate controls (No CF-No CF pairs) and rule out confounding by sensory error differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Statistical significance is established via bootstrap confidence intervals.

results.result: During VOR-decrease training, there was no trial-by-trial correlation between climbing fiber activity and changes in Purkinje cell output, despite gradual adaptive changes in Purkinje cell responses over the full training session. The same Purkinje cells that showed climbing fiber-dependent plasticity during VOR-increase training showed no such trial-by-trial effects during VOR-decrease training.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C61-C63, C65-C66 demonstrate a dissociation between climbing fiber activity and plasticity during VOR-decrease training. Figure 3D,E shows absence of trial-by-trial correlation, while Figure 4 demonstrates gradual learning-related changes occur over longer timescales. The within-cell comparison (same cells tested in both paradigms) strengthens the conclusion that climbing fiber efficacy is context-dependent. Lesion studies (C64) confirm these cells participate in VOR-decrease learning.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of climbing fibers during the ipsiversive phase of vestibular stimulation induced VOR-increase learning. The effect was long-lasting (persisting 2 hr post-training), graded with stimulation intensity (stronger with 3 vs 1 pulse per cycle), and significantly exceeded vestibular-only habituation controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C79-C80, C84, C87 are supported by optogenetic experiments in Figures 6-7 showing dose-dependent VOR-increase learning. Multiple stimulation protocols (bilateral/unilateral, 1x/3x pulses) all induced learning when timed to mimic VOR-increase training. Statistical comparisons to vestibular-only controls and measurements at multiple timepoints (immediate and 2hr) demonstrate robust, persistent effects. The graded response to stimulation intensity supports a causal relationship.

results.result: Optogenetic climbing fiber stimulation during the contraversive phase of vestibular stimulation did not induce VOR-decrease learning. Multiple stimulation protocols (1x and 3x pulses, unilateral and bilateral) all failed to produce associative VOR-decrease learning below vestibular-only habituation levels, either immediately or 2 hr post-training.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C82, C85-C86 are supported by negative results from optogenetic experiments (Figures 6-7). Despite testing multiple stimulation intensities and configurations, none induced VOR-decrease learning beyond habituation. The positive control showing visually-induced VOR-decrease learning was possible (C83) rules out a ceiling/floor effect. The same climbing fiber stimulation that induced robust VOR-increase learning had no effect when timed for VOR-decrease, supporting context-dependent gating.

results.result: The ability of climbing fibers to induce plasticity is dynamically gated in vivo, even when climbing fibers are robustly activated by performance errors. This gating occurs downstream of error encoding and represents a novel component of the cerebellar learning algorithm, with climbing fiber-triggered plasticity regulated at two stages: olivary spiking and the efficacy of climbing fiber spikes to induce plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C10, C90-C91, C96-C97, C103, C115, C117-C118 represent the main conclusion synthesizing results from both recording and optogenetic experiments. The conclusion is well-supported by: (1) equal climbing fiber error responses during both training paradigms (C32, C35, C50), (2) differential plasticity induction (VOR-increase: yes, VOR-decrease: no), (3) within-cell/within-animal comparisons ruling out individual differences, and (4) convergent evidence from trial-by-trial analysis and optogenetic manipulation. The two-stage gating model (C117) integrates current findings with prior work on olivary regulation.

results.result: Climbing fibers in the floccular complex encode retinal slip errors during both VOR-increase and VOR-decrease training with equal amplitude. The same climbing fibers respond to contraversive retinal slip in both paradigms, with increased firing probability 75-250 ms after stimulus onset. What distinguishes the paradigms is whether climbing fiber activation occurs during ipsiversive (VOR-increase) or contraversive (VOR-decrease) vestibular stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32, C35-C36, C47-C50 establish that climbing fiber error encoding is equivalent across paradigms. Figure 2E-F shows similar response amplitudes (t(9)=1.77, p=0.11), and all cells responding in one paradigm also responded in the other (C32). This is critical for interpreting the differential plasticity results—the gating cannot be explained by differences in error signal strength. The characterization is supported by both current data and extensive prior literature (C35, C43, C47).

results.result: Complex spike waveforms during VOR-decrease training had more spikelets and longer duration than during VOR-increase training, ruling out shorter complex spike duration as an explanation for reduced climbing fiber efficacy during VOR-decrease learning. Post-complex spike pause duration was similar between paradigms.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73, C105 are supported by waveform analysis in Figure 5A-B showing significantly longer complex spikes (more spikelets, longer duration, p<0.05) during VOR-decrease vs VOR-increase training. This finding is surprising given prior in vitro work (C70) suggesting shorter complex spikes reduce plasticity induction. The result rules out one potential mechanism for differential climbing fiber efficacy and suggests other circuit-level factors must be responsible.

results.result: Simple spike firing rate decreased relative to baseline during both training paradigms, but the reduction was smaller during VOR-decrease than VOR-increase training. This indicates no floor effect limiting plasticity during VOR-decrease training, but suggests different patterns of excitatory/inhibitory input that might regulate climbing fiber-triggered plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76, C108-C109 are supported by simple spike analysis in Figures 2G-H and 5C showing significant differences in firing rate modulation between paradigms (t(9)=3.39, p<0.01). The higher firing rate during VOR-decrease training rules out a floor effect (C75) and suggests differential E/I balance (C76, C109). However, the mechanistic link to plasticity gating remains speculative—the data show correlation but not causation.

results.result: Convergent evidence from trial-by-trial recordings and optogenetic stimulation demonstrates that climbing fiber error signals drive VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning. The same cells and animals showed context-dependent coupling between climbing fiber activity and plasticity induction, extending previous work to demonstrate selective contribution of all climbing fiber-dependent plasticity mechanisms (not just pf-Pk LTD) to VOR-increase learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89, C92-C93, C95, C100, C102, C114 synthesize the complementary evidence from recording (trial-by-trial) and manipulation (optogenetic) experiments. The within-subject design (C102) is particularly powerful for ruling out alternative explanations. The extension beyond pf-Pk LTD (C100) is important because optogenetic stimulation would recruit all climbing fiber-dependent mechanisms. The consistency across experimental approaches and timescales (C114) strengthens causal interpretation.

results.result: The convergent evidence from recording, stimulation, and previous perturbation studies strengthens interpretation of the results. VOR-increase learning provides a positive control demonstrating the experimental approaches could detect climbing fiber-triggered plasticity, which is critical for interpreting negative VOR-decrease results. The findings are consistent with previous work showing mice with impaired pf-Pk LTD are selectively impaired on VOR-increase but not VOR-decrease learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99, C101 address methodological considerations and integration with prior literature. The positive control argument (C101) is essential for interpreting negative results—the same methods that detected climbing fiber effects in VOR-increase failed to detect them in VOR-decrease, supporting genuine absence rather than methodological failure. Consistency with Boyden et al. 2006 (C99) provides independent validation using a different approach (genetic perturbation vs. recording/optogenetics).

results.result: Changes in Purkinje cell activity observed on single trials (~10% of average firing rate) are consistent in direction with changes observed over 90s training periods and after hours/days of training. The trial-by-trial analysis results parallel the optogenetic stimulation results across different timescales, suggesting mechanistic relationships between short-term and long-term plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111, C113-C114 address the relationship between plasticity at different timescales. The consistency in direction across timescales (C113) is well-documented with citations. However, the magnitude analysis (C111) reveals a puzzle: 10% changes per trial should accumulate to massive changes over 1000 trials, but observed learning is <50%, suggesting most single-trial changes decay rapidly. The claim of mechanistic relationship (C110) is supported by parallel findings but remains somewhat speculative regarding underlying mechanisms.

results.result: Recordings were made from 10 Purkinje cells in two rhesus monkeys during VOR training. For optogenetic experiments, AAV-ChR2 was injected into the inferior olive, and ChR2 expression in climbing fibers was verified anatomically and functionally via optrode recordings showing light-evoked complex spikes.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C77-C78 describe core methodological details. Sample size (n=10 cells, 2 monkeys) is stated clearly. Optogenetic validation (C78, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) is appropriate, demonstrating both anatomical expression and functional efficacy. However, the small sample size (2 animals, 10 cells) for the recording experiments is a limitation, though within-cell comparisons across paradigms partially mitigate this concern.

results.result: The VOR circuit involves vestibular inputs driving eye movements through vestibular nuclei, with cerebellar modulation via Purkinje cells that receive parallel fiber and climbing fiber inputs. Climbing fibers encode retinal slip errors, and VOR gain can be adaptively increased or decreased through motor learning that depends on the cerebellar floccular complex. Purkinje cell recordings provide simultaneous access to climbing fiber activity (complex spikes) and Purkinje cell output (simple spikes).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26, C33-C34, C42-C46 provide essential background on VOR circuitry and learning paradigms. These are well-established facts supported by extensive prior literature (multiple citations) and illustrated in Figures 1-2. The description of recording methodology (C25-C26, C42) is standard and well-validated. This background is necessary context but not a novel finding of the current study.

results.result: The cerebellum is thought to implement supervised learning with climbing fibers providing error signals, but evidence has been conflicting. Climbing fibers are activated by errors during many tasks, reliably trigger complex spikes, and can induce plasticity in vitro and replace teaching signals in vivo. However, some studies show dissociations between error encoding and learning, and perturbation of pf-Pk LTD has inconsistent effects across tasks. Recent work suggests Purkinje cell responses to climbing fibers can be graded, potentially regulating plasticity induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C19 provide literature review establishing the controversial state of the field regarding climbing fiber roles in learning. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to prior work. This contextualizes why the current study's question (whether climbing fiber efficacy is gated in vivo) is important and unresolved. The review accurately represents both supporting and conflicting evidence from prior literature.

results.result: Prior work has shown that Purkinje cell responses change during VOR learning in a manner consistent with climbing fiber-triggered LTD or potentiation of inhibition. Optogenetic climbing fiber activation can induce VOR-increase learning, but previous attempts at VOR-decrease learning failed. Studies of pf-Pk LTD mutants show inconsistent VOR learning impairments. Mossy fiber inputs and Purkinje cell responses are present during both contraversive and ipsiversive vestibular stimuli. Complex spike duration and inhibitory input levels can regulate climbing fiber-induced plasticity in reduced preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40, C52-C56, C64, C67-C70, C104, C106-C107, C116 review relevant prior findings that inform interpretation of current results. All are appropriately cited. These establish: (1) expected circuit mechanisms (C52-C55), (2) prior evidence for climbing fiber roles (C37-C38, C56), (3) prior negative results (C39-C40), (4) availability of synaptic substrates (C67-C69), and (5) potential regulatory mechanisms (C70, C104, C106-C107). This contextualizes the current findings within existing literature.

results.result: VOR-increase training pairs visual stimuli with vestibular stimuli in opposite directions, while VOR-decrease training pairs them in the same direction. Both paradigms produce retinal slip reflecting performance errors.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 describe the training paradigms illustrated in Figure 2A-D. These are standard, well-established VOR training protocols appropriately cited to prior literature. The description is accurate and necessary for understanding the experimental design.

results.result: VOR gain increased between end of training and 2hr retest for both optogenetic VOR-increase and vestibular-only training, presumably reflecting decay of non-associative habituation. Visual-vestibular VOR-decrease training produced greater VOR gain decrease than vestibular-only training, demonstrating associative VOR-decrease learning was possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C83 describe control observations. C81 (habituation decay) is supported by data in Figures 6B and 7, though the mechanistic explanation is speculative. C83 provides an important positive control (Figure 7A) demonstrating that VOR-decrease learning is possible in these animals when appropriate sensory feedback is provided, ruling out a general inability to undergo VOR-decrease learning. Both claims are well-supported by data.

results.result: Dynamic gating of neural error signals controlling learning induction may be a general feature of neural learning algorithms and merits systematic investigation in cerebellum and other circuits. Defining factors influencing cerebellar receptivity to error signals will be critical for developing learning theories and strategies to optimize plasticity for learning or recovery from injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are speculative statements about broader implications and future directions. While the speculation is reasonable given the findings, these claims go beyond what the data directly support. C119 generalizes from one specific case (VOR learning) to all neural learning algorithms without supporting evidence. C120 makes claims about future importance that cannot be evaluated from current data. These are appropriate discussion points but not supported results.
